sentences.text: Revenue, net interest income plus noninterest income, rose from $21.0 billion in FY2016 to $28.5 billion in FY2025, a 3.5% CAGR [D5][D219].
The path was a step change rather than compounding: revenue was $22.7 billion in FY2021 and $28.0 billion in FY2023 [D117][D169].
The FY2023 step came from higher rates on earning assets and the MUB acquisition, which lifted net interest income 18.1% [D184][P33].
FY2022 was the other inflection, with net interest income up 17.9% on rising rates and MUB balances [D159][P44].
Consumer and Business Banking was the largest segment at 31.0% of FY2025 revenue but shrank 3.9%, subtracting 1.3pp from growth [D251][D252][D253].
That decline came from deposit mix and second-quarter loan sales, which cut segment net interest income 4.9% [P6].
Payment Services grew 5.4% and added 1.4pp, with net revenue up 5.4% on higher merchant processing and card revenue [D260][D261][P4].
Net income grew 20.2% in FY2025 against 4.4% revenue growth, and EPS grew 21.9% as the diluted share count fell 0.2% [D227][D239][D229][D237].
Noninterest expense fell 2.0% in FY2025 while revenue grew 4.4% [D238][D239].
The efficiency ratio was 59.0% in FY2025, above the 55.3% window low and below the 59.3% median [D220][D275][D277].
The FY2023 peak of 67.4% reflected merger and integration charges, the FDIC special assessment and MUB operating expenses [D276][P30].
The FY2025 fall to 59.0% came from prior-year merger and FDIC charges dropping out and lower compensation [D220][P10].
In FY2025 net margin of 26.5% sat 32.5pp below the 59.0% efficiency ratio, with a 20.2% tax rate and a 7.7% provision [D223][D220][D215][D221].
Operating cash flow of $8.0 billion was 1.05x net income in FY2025, below the 1.80x of FY2024 [F60][D216][D191].
Operating cash flow is not a meaningful earnings-quality measure for a bank; capital return of $3.7 billion was 48.3% of net income [D218][F30].
Stock-based compensation was 2.9% of operating cash flow, up from 2.0% [D217][D192].
Return on average equity was 12.2%, above the 11.8% peer median and in the 71st percentile of seven banks [D226][D283][D282].
Loans were 73.5% of deposits, up from 71.8%, and the allowance was 2.0% of loans [D224][D199][D225].
Buybacks plus dividends of $3.7 billion were below the $7.0 billion of FY2019, and buybacks fell to $489 million from $4.5 billion [D218][D65][X85][X79].
Long-term debt was last reported at $39.8 billion in FY2022 and is not reported after that year [X172][R2].
Long-term debt is not reported after FY2022, a data break that prevents a debt comparison across the window [R2][X172].
This is a disclosure gap rather than a credit event, but it leaves the funding trend unverifiable.
Revenue declined in FY2024, with net interest income down 6.4% [R1][D209].
The decline came from higher rates on deposit mix and pricing, partly offset by earning-asset growth [P20].
The FY2025 rebound to 4.4% growth suggests the pressure was cyclical rather than structural [D239].
If the efficiency ratio moves back above the 59.3% window median, the FY2025 cost improvement would be reversing [D277].
If net interest income growth falls below the FY2025 2.2%, the loan-growth and funding-cost tailwind would be fading [D234].
If the credit-loss provision rises above the 7.7% of revenue seen in FY2025, credit quality would be deteriorating [D221].
